title: Senior's toolkit: certificates in .NET
summary: The dev-cert commands, Kestrel settings and X509 APIs a .NET engineer uses to ship HTTPS and trust a private CA.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: certificates in .NET
steps.body: You have built a CA in code. These are the commands and APIs you use to run HTTPS in real .NET services, locally and in containers.

toolkit.what: Exports the development certificate and its key as PEM files, for a container or a non-.NET tool.
flags: PEM instead of PFX; with a password or `--no-password` the key goes in the same folder with a `.key` extension (`localhost.key`)
leave the exported key unencrypted (dev only)
toolkit.when: running an ASP.NET Core container with HTTPS on your laptop

toolkit.what: Points Kestrel at a certificate from the environment, so the same image runs with a different certificate in each environment.
flags: the PFX or key password (from a secret store)

toolkit.what: On Linux .NET uses OpenSSL, which reads these variables. Point them at a bundle that includes your private root to trust it without code changes.
flags: one PEM bundle of trusted roots

toolkit.what: Loads a PEM certificate and its key into one object you can use for TLS or signing.
flags: the PEM certificate (first block is the leaf)
the PEM key; omit when it is in the same file

toolkit.what: The current way (.NET 9 and later) to load a PFX. The old `new X509Certificate2(path, password)` constructor is obsolete (SYSLIB0057).
flags: a certificate with no key (PEM or DER)
keep the key in memory only

toolkit.what: Validates a chain against your own root only, ignoring the machine store. The right way to trust a private CA in code.
flags: intermediates that help build the path

toolkit.what: Makes a test certificate in the Windows store from PowerShell, for an IIS site or a quick local test.
flags: the names for the SAN list

steps.prompt: Match each API or setting to its job.
pairs: load a PEM certificate with its key
load a PFX the current way
the roots your chain check trusts
intermediates that help build the path
tell Kestrel which certificate to serve

steps.prompt: Your service runs fine on your Windows laptop, but in its Linux container `HttpClient` calls to `https://billing.corp.internal` fail with `The remote certificate is invalid ... UntrustedRoot`. The billing certificate comes from the company CA. What is the right fix?
options: Add the company root to the image's trust store (copy it to `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/` and run `update-ca-certificates`)
steps.explain: Your laptop trusts the company root because IT installed it in Windows; the container image does not. Install the root in the image (or point `SSL_CERT_FILE` at a bundle with it). The other options remove TLS protection.

steps.prompt: Validate `leaf` against your own root only, with the intermediate as a helper.
steps.explain: `CustomRootTrust` ignores the machine store. Roots go in `CustomTrustStore`; intermediates in `ExtraStore` are used to build the path but are not trusted by themselves.

steps.prompt: After moving to .NET 10 the build warns `SYSLIB0057` on `new X509Certificate2("api.pfx", password)`. What do you change it to?
steps.explain: The loader makes the format explicit, so a file cannot be parsed as something you did not expect. `CreateFromPemFile` is for PEM, not PFX.

steps.prompt: Fine for local development only, or fine in production?
items: Kestrel certificate paths from environment variables and mounted secrets
a company root installed in the image with `update-ca-certificates`

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Keep certificates out of the image and the repository: mount them and point Kestrel at them through configuration. When a call fails only in a container, compare trust stores before you touch code, and never ship a callback that returns `true`.
